entries.test: Historical records of research activity, investment, and commercial adoption would show whether the current neural-network revival had sustained itself more strongly than the earlier revival by February 2023.
entries.note: The comparison concerns the revivals as assessed at publication.

entries.test: Comparing the cited historical criticisms with public evaluations of models available in February 2023 would establish whether compositionality, abstraction, and basic errors remained recurring problems.
entries.note: The surrounding text identifies the concerns, making the claim testable.

entries.test: Public evaluations across contemporary LLMs would show whether basic errors persisted and abstraction failures were widespread in February 2023.

entries.note: “Seems to underlie” presents a tentative causal explanation; “appear to stem” preserves that hedge.

entries.test: Public results available by February 2023 would show whether deep learning had progressed in image generation and conversation while leaving abstraction, compositionality, and the type-token distinction unresolved.
entries.note: The preceding sentences explicitly define “hit a wall” in this limited sense.

entries.test: A publicly demonstrated AGI that still lacked solutions to abstraction, compositionality, or the type-token distinction would refute the asserted prerequisite.
entries.note: The claim makes reaching AGI conditional on solving the named problems and supplies no deadline.

entries.test: The referenced compositionality study and historical studies would show whether the modern model exhibited the same kind of compositionality failure as earlier models.
entries.note: The immediate wording concerns a particular study and model; the normalization broadens it to modern architectures generally. The study's abstract is absent from the supplied text.

entries.test: Razeghi’s arithmetic results and comparable public evaluations would show whether contemporary LLMs continued to fail arithmetic abstraction despite changed architectures and training regimes.
Historical descriptions of neural-model limitations and public evaluations of February 2023 models would establish whether some of the same basic problems persisted.
entries.note: Read in context, “basic issues” refers to some recurring limitations, not every historical criticism.

entries.test: Public reporting on outsourced AI annotation and feedback work, its pay and working conditions, and its role in correcting model behavior would test the asserted shift to low-wage human patching.
entries.note: He asserts the outsourcing comparison but expresses uncertainty about how much the broader reliance on hacks has changed. The normalization makes that broader continuity categorical.

entries.test: Public staffing, contracting, and expenditure records would show whether AI companies spent substantial sums on human correction of neural systems in the early 2020s and symbolic systems in the 1980s.
entries.note: These are Marcus’s own embedded words; the subsequent Alexandr Wang quotation is a separate attribution.

entries.test: Comparative evaluations and public deployment reports would show whether February 2023 AI systems improved on predecessors yet frequently failed real-world tasks they appeared capable of handling in laboratory demonstrations.
entries.note: The lab-versus-deployment comparison gives “superficial” a testable operational reading.
“Probably” explicitly qualifies the forecast. The passage also separately asserts that edge-case failures were the norm at publication.
